newsitem.title: UK: New UN boss welcomed in most European capitals.
newsitem.headline: New UN boss welcomed in most European capitals.

text.p: Europeans gave a warm welcome on Saturday to the appointment of Ghana's Kofi Annan as the next secretary-general of the United Nations, praising his skills and experience as a professional administrator.
Only France, which reluctantly fell in with other permanent U.N.Security Council members, seemed grudging in its response.
Annan, 58, was chosen by the Security Council on Friday to succeed Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali, whose hopes for a second term were derailed by Washington.

The career diplomat, currently U.N. undersecretary-general for peacekeeping operations, won the support of all 15 Security Council members after France dropped its veto threat. His selection now has to be ratified by the General Assembly.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette hinted to reporters at a European Union summit in Dublin that France may have sought the number two job at the U.N. in return for dropping its opposition to Annan.
One of the five permanent Security Council powers with the right to veto candidates, France was the last of the 15 Council members to hold out against Annan in test votes this week.

Asked whether Paris wanted the deputy secretary-general job for a Frenchman, de Charette said: "We made known to Mr Kofi Annan our support, we reminded him what our concerns were, in particular our attachment to bilingualism, not only in the person of the secretary-general but also in the practice and daily life and the work of the United Nations."
"We added that we wanted France and Francophone countries to have their fair share of responsibility in the echelons of the U.N. and, it goes without saying, in the secretariat."
De Charette said France had had doubts about Annan's ability to reform the United Nations vigorously after having spent so many years at the centre of the organisation.
In contrast, British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind was effusive in his welcoming statement.

"I have the highest regard for Mr Annan, with whom we have worked very closely for many years," Rifkind said. "He has enormous experience...including administration and finance as well as the key political issues.

"His experience and outstanding personal qualities make him ideally qualified to lead the U.N. in tackling the many urgent tasks which it currently faces. I am sure that he will fill this vitally important post with great distinction. The British government will give him its full support," he said.
Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Vasily Sidorov told Interfax news agency that Moscow supported Annan.
"He is a top-level professional," said Sidorov, adding Annan's priority should be reorganising the United Nations and adapting it to realities of the next century.
Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen said Annan had done a "very good job" in his previous posts.
"I know him well from his work at the U.N...I think he has done a good job there," she told Sweden's news agency TT.
Austria described Annan as an exceptional man.
"He is an exceptional man who has made himself an excellent name throughout the U.N.," Benita Ferrero-Waldner, state secretary in the Austrian Foreign Ministry, said in a statement.
Several Italian newspapers emphasised that the Security Council's decision to name Annan as U.N. secretary-general was a big defeat for Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who served only one term.
La Repubblica posed the question whether Annan would be able to carry out the reforms that everyone seemed to want.
The newspaper said the United States, having backed Annan, would now have to live up to its commitments to the U.N., referring to late payment of dues.
"Now the United States has to respect their duties in their dealings with the 'U.N. family'," La Repubblica said.

In the Netherlands, de Volkskrant newspaper commented: "Annan's ability to present himself as a diplomat...rather than a world leader, is undoubtedly, for the U.S., an important reason to support him. America wants a sort of 'super-clerk' as secretary-general. Whether Annan wants to play that role remains to be seen.
"With the U.N. facing so much criticism...Annan faces the unenviable task of convincing the world that he is a diplomat, manager, humanist and visionary all at the same time."
